Within a strategy, use a namespace to specify AgentCore Memory organizes long-term memories.\\n\\nEvery time AgentCore Memory extracts a new long-term memory with a memory strategy, the long-term memory is saved under the namespace that you specify. This means that all long-term memories are scoped to their specific namespace, keeping them organized and preventing any conflicts with other users or sessions. Structure the namespace as a hierarchy of segments separated by forward slashes `/`, with a leading and a trailing slash. The slash prevents prefix collisions in multi-tenant applications\u2014for example, use `/actors/alice/` instead of `/actors/alice`. As needed, you can use the following pre-defined variables within braces in the namespace based on your application\u2019s organization needs:\\n\\n* **actorId** \u2013 Identifies who the long-term memory belongs to.\\n* **strategyId** \u2013 Shows which memory strategy is being used.\\n* **sessionId** \u2013 Identifies which session or conversation the memory is from.\\n\\nFor example, if you define the following namespace as the input to your strategy when creating an AgentCore Memory:\\n\\n```\\n/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/session/{sessionId}/\\n```\\n\\nAfter memory creation, this namespace might look like:\\n\\n```\\n/strategy/summarization-93483043/actor/actor-9830m2w3/session/session-9330sds8/\\n```\\n\\nA namespace can have different levels of granularity:\\n\\n**Most granular Level of organization**\\n\\n`/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/session/{sessionId}/`\\n\\n**Granular at the actor Level across sessions**\\n\\n`/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/`\\n\\n**Granular at the strategy Level across actors**\\n\\n`/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/`\\n\\n**Global across all strategies**\\n\\n`/`\\n\\nFor example code, see Enable long-term memory.\\n\\nFor more information about organizing long-term memories with namespaces, including custom namespace variables, see Specify long-term memory organization with namespaces\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory-organization.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Specify long-term memory organization with namespaces\",\"context\":\"# Specify long-term memory organization with namespaces\\n\\nWhen you create an AgentCore Memory, use a namespace to specify where the long-term memories for a memory strategy are logically grouped. Every time a new long-term memory is extracted using the memory strategy, it is saved under the namespace you set. This means that all long-term memories are scoped to their specific namespace, keeping them organized and preventing any mix-ups with other users or sessions. You should use a hierarchical format separated by forward slashes `/`, starting and ending with a slash (for example, `/actors/alice/`). This helps keep memories organized clearly. As needed, you can choose to use the following pre-defined variables within braces in the namespace based on your application\u2019s organization needs:\\n\\n* **actorId** \u2013 Identifies who the long-term memory belongs to.\\n\\n An actor refers to entity such as end users or agent/user combinations. For example, in a coding support chatbot, the actor is usually the developer asking questions. Using the actor ID helps the system know which user the memory belongs to, keeping each user\u2019s data separate and organized.\\n* **strategyId** \u2013 Shows which memory strategy is being used. This strategy identifier is auto-generated when you create an AgentCore Memory.\\n* **sessionId** \u2013 Identifies which session or conversation the memory is from.\\n\\n A session is usually a single conversation or interaction period between the user and the AI agent. It groups all related messages and events that happen during that conversation.\\n\\nFor example, if you define the following namespace as the input to your strategy when creating an AgentCore Memory:\\n\\n```\\n/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/session/{sessionId}/\\n```\\n\\nAfter memory creation, this namespace might look like:\\n\\n```\\n/strategy/summarization-93483043/actor/actor-9830m2w3/session/session-9330sds8/\\n```\\n\\nA namespace can have different levels of granularity. The following examples use built-in variables only:\\n\\n**Granular at the session level**\\n\\n`/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/session/{sessionId}/`\\n\\n**Granular at the actor level across sessions**\\n\\n`/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/actor/{actorId}/`\\n\\n**Granular at the strategy level across actors**\\n\\n`/strategy/{memoryStrategyId}/`\\n\\n**Global across all strategies**\\n\\n`/`\\n\\nFor even more granular organization, you can add custom namespace variables to represent additional dimensions such as tenant\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/specify-long-term-memory-organization.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Use agentic retrieval to query a knowledge base\",\"context\":\"## Use AgentCore Memory with agentic retrieval\\n\\nYou can give agentic retrieval access to an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory\\nresource. With memory access, a retrieval can continue an earlier session and draw on\\nwhat the agent has learned in previous ones. Supply the\\n`memoryConfiguration` field with the `memoryId` of a memory\\nresource in your account that is in the `ACTIVE` state.\\n\\nMemory is optional. A `memoryConfiguration` that sets only a\\n`memoryId` is not valid. When you supply\\n`memoryConfiguration`, you must use the memory resource in at least one of\\nthe following two ways:\\n\\n* **Short-term memory**\\n (`sessionBinding`)\u2014Restores the history of an earlier session\\n so that the request continues that session instead of starting fresh. Identify the\\n records with a `namespace` prefix, or with a\\n `namespacePath` to retrieve across every namespace beneath a parent.\\n You can narrow the results further with a `strategyId` and with\\n `metadataFilters`. For more information about namespaces, strategies, and memory\\nrecords, see Memory\\nterminology in the *Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide*.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nYou are responsible for supplying the correct `memoryId`,\\n`sessionBinding`, and `retrievalConfigs` values. Agentic\\nretrieval does not verify that the session or the namespaces\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-agentic-retrieve.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Memory\",\"context\":\"## Long-term memory retrieval\\n\\nWhen a harness has active memory strategies (managed or BYO), retrieval works automatically - the harness derives a retrieval configuration from the Memory instance\u2019s active strategies. On each invocation, the agent queries relevant long-term memories and injects them into the conversation context before reasoning.\\n\\n**Default behavior:**\\n\\n* Retrieval is configured automatically with default parameters (`topK=10`, `relevanceScore=0.2`) for each active strategy\u2019s namespace.\\n* No manual configuration needed for either managed or BYO memory.\\n\\n**Override the defaults:** If you explicitly provide a `retrievalConfig` in the BYO memory configuration, your values take priority and no automatic derivation occurs. By default, memory events (which we refer to as short-term memory) can be written to an AgentCore Memory. For insights to be extracted and placed into long term memory records, the resource requires a *memory strategy* which is a configuration that defines how conversational data should be processed, and what information to extract (such as facts, preferences, or summaries).\\n\\nIn this step, you create an AgentCore Memory with a semantic strategy so that both short term and long term memory can be utilized. This will take 2-3 minutes. You can also create AgentCore Memory resources in the AWS console.\\n\\nCreate memory with semantic strategy:\\n\\n###### Example\\n\\n#### Using AgentCore CLI\\n\\n1. ```\\n agentcore add memory --name CustomerSupportSemantic --strategies SEMANTIC\\n\\n agentcore deploy\\n ```\\n\\n#### Using Interactive\\n\\n1. Run `agentcore add memory` to open the Memory wizard.\\n2. Enter the memory name, such as `CustomerSupportSemantic`.\\n3. Use the arrow keys and Space to select `SEMANTIC`, then press Enter.\\n4. Keep the default event retention of 30 days, review the configuration, and press Enter to add the memory.\\n\\n5. Press Ctrl+C to exit the TUI, then run `agentcore deploy` to provision the memory in AWS.\\n\\nAfter deployment, run `agentcore status --json` and copy the memory `arn`. The memory ID is the part of the ARN after `memory/`. Then check that the memory status is `ACTIVE`:\\n\\n```\\nagentcore status --json\\nagentcore memory get --id <memory-id>\\n```\\n\\n## Step 2: Write events to memory\\n\\nYou can write events to an AgentCore Memory as short-term memory and extracts insights for long-term memory.\\n\\nWriting events to memory has multiple purposes. First, event contents (most commonly conversation history) are stored as short-term memory. Second, relevant insights are pulled from events and written into memory records as a part of long-term memory.\\n\\nThe memory resource id, actor id, and session id are required to create an event. In this step, you create three events, simulating messages between an end user and a chat bot. Replace `<your-memory-id>` with the memory ID from Step 1.\\n\\n```\\nfrom bedrock_agentcore.memory import MemorySessionManager\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory-get-started.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AgentCore long-term memory strategy and retrieval docs"}

You usually have to write events, read them back and pass them to the model yourself. These are the checks I'd run, most common causes first.

**1. Confirm events are being written**
- Check that the agent calls `CreateEvent` (or uses a session manager or hook that does) after each turn. Both the user and assistant messages need to be saved.
- Run `agentcore memory event list --id <memory-id> --actor-id <actor> --session-id <session>`. If it returns nothing, writes are failing or going to a different memory ID. Look for swallowed exceptions or IAM `AccessDenied` errors in the agent's logs.
- Check that the memory status is `ACTIVE`. Also check the event retention period, which defaults to 30 days.

**2. Make sure actorId and sessionId stay the same across turns**
This is the most common cause. Events are keyed by `actorId` and `sessionId`.
- If the agent generates a new `sessionId` on each invocation, every turn looks like a new conversation. Pass one stable ID from the client on every call. On AgentCore Runtime, that is typically the runtime session ID.
- The same applies to `actorId`. It must be stable per user and not change between requests.
- `sessionId` is at most 100 characters. `actorId` is at most 255 characters and has a character pattern. Invalid values can cause failed writes.

**3. Make sure the history is read back and given to the model**
- Writing events doesn't load them. On each turn, the agent has to call `ListEvents` (or use a session manager or hook that does) with the same actor and session IDs. It then has to put those messages into the model's context.
- Check that the call isn't capped to a very small number of events or turns.
- Runtime containers can restart, and sessions aren't guaranteed to land on the same instance. Don't rely on in-process state. Load the history from Memory at the start of each turn.

**4. Separate short-term from long-term expectations**
- Short-term memory is the raw event history for one session. It gives you in-session continuity once the reads in step 3 work.
- Long-term memory only exists if you attached a memory strategy, such as semantic, summarization or user preference. Without one, nothing carries across sessions.
- Extraction into long-term records is asynchronous. A fact from the previous turn may not be retrievable yet.
- Retrieval has to be done explicitly with a namespace. For example, run `agentcore memory record list --id <memory-id> --namespace-path /` to see whether any records exist.

**5. Check namespaces and retrieval settings**
- The namespace you query must match the strategy's namespace, with the variables resolved. For example, use `/strategy/<id>/actor/<actorId>/`, not the template. The leading and trailing slashes matter.
- If a namespace includes `{sessionId}`, memories from other sessions won't be found. Use an actor-level namespace for cross-session recall.
- Check `topK` and the relevance score threshold. A threshold that is too high returns nothing. Harness defaults are `topK=10` and `relevanceScore=0.2`.
- If you use a harness with BYO memory and changed the strategies afterwards, run `UpdateHarness` to refresh the retrieval config.

**6. Check IAM and the region**
- The agent's execution role needs the data-plane permissions `bedrock-agentcore:CreateEvent`, `ListEvents`, `RetrieveMemoryRecords` and `ListMemoryRecords`, scoped to the memory ARN.
- Confirm the SDK client uses the same region and account as the memory.

**7. Check the framework wiring**
If you use Strands, LangGraph or a similar framework, check that the AgentCore memory session manager or checkpointer is attached to the agent instance that handles the request. A new agent object created per request without a session manager has no history.

**Fastest way to narrow it down**
After a two-turn test, run `agentcore memory event list` for the actor and session.
- **No events:** the problem is on the write side (steps 1, 2 and 6).
- **Events present, but the agent still forgets:** the problem is on the read side (steps 3 and 7).
- **Events present, but the facts don't carry across sessions:** the problem is long-term memory (steps 4 and 5).

If you send me the memory ID and runtime or agent name, I can check the account's logs and IAM setup. One of the agents here could be the affected one. Tell me whether the forgetting happens within a session or across sessions, which narrows the cause further.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
